listeningParts.title: Hiring an electric car
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a car hire company to book an electric car for a weekend trip.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, GreenWheels Car Hire, Martin speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Hi. I'd like to hire an electric car for a long weekend later this month, but I've never actually driven one before, so I've got quite a few questions.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No problem at all. Lots of our customers are first-time electric drivers. When would you need the car?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: From Friday the fourteenth to Monday the seventeenth. I'd collect it on the Friday morning and bring it back on Monday afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Let me just check the system. Yes, that's fine, we have cars available on those dates. At the moment we offer two models. The smaller one is the City, which is a five-door hatchback. It can travel about two hundred and eighty kilometres on a full charge. The larger one is the Tourer, which has much more space for luggage and a range of around four hundred and fifty kilometres.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: We're driving to the coast, which is about three hundred kilometres from here, so I suppose the Tourer would be better.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: I'd definitely recommend it. You could do the trip in the City, but you'd have to stop and charge on the way. And bear in mind that in cold weather the range drops, sometimes by as much as twenty per cent, because the heater and the battery itself use more energy when it's cold.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Oh, I didn't know that. The Tourer, then. How much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The Tourer is sixty-two pounds a day, so for four days that comes to two hundred and forty-eight pounds. The City would have been forty-five pounds a day, just so you know.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That's fine. Does the price include insurance?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Basic insurance is included, but there's an excess of eight hundred pounds. That means if the car is damaged, you'd pay up to eight hundred pounds yourself. You can reduce the excess to zero by paying an extra nine pounds a day.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I think I'll take that. I'd rather not have to worry about it on holiday.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Very sensible. Now, charging. The car will be fully charged when you collect it. Some companies ask you to bring the car back with at least eighty per cent, but we only ask for seventy. If it's below that, there's a fee of fifteen pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: And how do I pay when I charge on the road? Do I need to set up accounts with different companies?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No, the car comes with a charging card that works at most public chargers in the country. You just hold it against the charger, and the cost is added to your bill when you return the car.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That's easy. How long does charging take?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It depends on the charger. At a rapid charger, like the ones at motorway service stations, you can go from ten to eighty per cent in about thirty-five minutes, which is long enough for a coffee and a sandwich. At a normal charger, like the ones you find in hotel car parks, it takes about seven hours, so leaving it overnight is ideal.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: I think our hotel has chargers. Will I need my own cable?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No, there's a cable in the boot. It's stored under the floor panel, so it's easy to miss, but it's definitely there.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Good to know. Is there anything else that's different about driving an electric car?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Two main things. First, it's very quiet, so watch out for pedestrians who might not hear you coming, especially in car parks. Second, when you lift your foot off the accelerator, the car slows down quite strongly, because the motor is recharging the battery. It takes a few minutes to get used to, but most people end up loving it.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Okay, I'm convinced. Can I book it now?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. Can I take your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Joanna Whitcombe. That's W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you, Ms Whitcombe. And where would you like to collect the car from? We have two branches, one at the railway station and one on Canal Street.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: The station would be easier for me, because I'll be arriving by train.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Fine. The station branch opens at eight. When you come, please bring your driving licence and a credit card. I'm afraid we can't accept debit cards for the deposit, because we need to be able to hold the money for a few days.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: No problem. I've got both. Thanks so much for all your help, Martin.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: You're welcome. I'll email the confirmation to you within the hour. Enjoy your trip to the coast.

listeningParts.title: A tour of a former nuclear power station
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide welcomes visitors to an energy centre on the site of a nuclear power station that is being dismantled.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Hollins Bay Energy Centre. My name's Declan, and I'll be your guide this morning. Before we set off, I'd like to give you a little background about the site and explain what we'll be seeing on the tour.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Hollins Bay power station opened in 1968, and for more than forty years it generated electricity from nuclear power. At its peak, it supplied enough electricity for around one and a half million homes. It stopped generating in 2012, and since then it's been going through a process called decommissioning, which simply means taking the plant apart safely and cleaning up the site. People are often surprised to hear how long that takes.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The fuel was removed from the reactors during the first four years, and that was by far the most important stage, because the fuel contained more than ninety-nine per cent of the radioactivity on the site. Once it had gone, the risks dropped enormously. However, the full process of dismantling the buildings and returning the land to other uses is not expected to finish until the 2080s.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Visitors often ask why it takes so long. The main reason is that some of the materials inside the reactor buildings will remain radioactive for decades. It's actually safer, and cheaper, to wait for that radioactivity to decline naturally before workers go in and take the structures apart. So the reactor buildings themselves will be sealed and monitored for many years. You'll see them from outside, but nobody goes into them now except specialist teams.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: But this site isn't only about the past. In 2021, part of the land was used to build a large battery storage facility, which we call the Battery Park. You might wonder why it was put here, rather than somewhere closer to a city. The answer is that because the power station was connected to the national grid, the heavy cables and connections were already in place, which saved a great deal of money and time. The batteries store electricity when there's plenty of wind power, often during the night, and then release it when demand is highest, which is usually in the early evening, when people get home and start cooking.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: One more thing before we start. Around a third of our guides used to work in the power station itself, as engineers or technicians, so if you have detailed questions about how it operated, please do ask them. They know far more than I do.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, let me tell you about the route. We'll begin in the Exhibition Hall, just behind me. It has lots of interactive displays, including a simulator where you can try to balance supply and demand on the electricity grid. Children love it, though it's much harder than it looks. The entrance building that you came through, by the way, was rebuilt only last year, after a storm damaged the roof.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: From there, we'll go across to the Turbine Hall. This is the largest building on the site, and the giant turbines are still in place. Because it's a working area for the decommissioning team, everybody will need to wear a hard hat, which we'll hand out at the door. Please don't remove it until you're outside again.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next is the Control Room, which has been kept exactly as it was on the day the station closed, right down to the logbooks on the desks. It's quite small, so we'll go in groups of ten. Unfortunately, it's at the top of a narrow staircase and there's no lift, so it can't be reached by wheelchair users. However, there's a video tour of it in the Exhibition Hall, so nobody needs to miss out.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: After that, we'll walk to the Viewing Gallery on the roof of the old administration block. From there, you get wonderful views right along the coast, and on a clear day you can see the offshore wind farm, about twelve kilometres out to sea.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, we'll finish at the Battery Park. For security reasons, we ask you not to take any photographs there, although you're very welcome to take pictures everywhere else on the tour. The whole tour lasts about ninety minutes. Afterwards, the café by the entrance is open, although only at weekends during the winter. Right, if you'd like to follow me.

listeningParts.title: Recycling electric car batteries
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two engineering students, Tom and Mei, discuss their project on battery recycling with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, both of you. So, you've chosen to look at what happens to electric car batteries at the end of their lives. How's the research going?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. We started by trying to work out how big the problem will be. At the moment, the number of electric car batteries reaching the end of their life is still quite small, because most electric cars on the road are fairly new. But by the 2030s, the numbers are expected to rise very steeply.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: And one thing we hadn't realised is that a battery that's no longer good enough for a car isn't actually dead. Car makers usually consider a battery worn out when it can only hold around seventy to eighty per cent of its original charge, because the driving range becomes too short. But it can still be perfectly useful for other things.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: You mean what's called second-life use?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Exactly. Old car batteries can be combined and used for stationary storage, for example to store solar power for a building. Weight and size don't matter much there, so a lower capacity is acceptable. We visited a company that does this, and they said a battery can often work for another ten years or so.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's interesting, but does that simply delay the recycling problem?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: It does, yes, and some people argue it's better to recycle straight away, so the materials get back into new car batteries sooner. That's one of the questions we want to discuss in the report.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And what about the recycling itself? What methods did you look at?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: There are two main ones at the moment. The first is basically smelting: the batteries are put into a furnace at very high temperatures, and metals like cobalt, nickel and copper are recovered. It's a well-established process, but it uses a lot of energy, and most of the lithium ends up in a waste product called slag, where it's difficult to recover.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: The second method is to discharge the batteries, take them apart and shred them. That produces a dark powder that the industry calls black mass, which contains the valuable metals. Then chemicals are used to dissolve the metals and separate them. It uses less energy and recovers more of the lithium, but it involves strong acids, so the waste water has to be treated carefully.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And is there anything newer on the horizon?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Yes, researchers are working on what's called direct recycling, where the cathode material is repaired and reused without breaking it down into separate metals. It could be much cheaper, but it's still mostly at the laboratory stage.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What did you find was the biggest practical obstacle?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Honestly, it's the design of the batteries. Manufacturers use strong glues to hold the cells together, so taking a battery pack apart can take a skilled worker several hours. And every manufacturer's packs are different, so it's very hard to automate.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a good point to make. And there's a safety issue too, isn't there?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Definitely. A damaged battery can catch fire, and the fires are very hard to put out. Actually, recycling centres say the bigger problem at the moment is small batteries from things like phones and vapes that people throw away with their ordinary rubbish. They get crushed in the lorries and start fires.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So what's the case for recycling? Why does it matter so much?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Partly it's environmental, of course, but there's also the question of supply. A small number of countries control a large share of the mining and processing of these metals. Around seventy per cent of the world's cobalt, for example, is mined in one country, the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Recycling could make countries less dependent on imports.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. Now, for the next stage, I'd like you to compare the costs of the two main methods. And please contact the recycling plant near Coventry. They've helped students before.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: We'll email them this week. Should we include a section on government policy?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, briefly. The European Union has introduced rules requiring new batteries to contain a minimum share of recycled material in future, so mention those. Keep it to about a page, though.

listeningParts.title: The quest for fusion power
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a physics and energy course about nuclear fusion and the challenges of using it to generate electricity.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Last week we looked at nuclear fission, the process used in every nuclear power station operating today, in which heavy atoms such as uranium are split apart. Today I want to turn to the opposite process, nuclear fusion, which many people regard as the ultimate source of clean energy, and explain why it has proved so extraordinarily difficult to achieve.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Fusion is the process that powers the Sun and every other star. In the Sun's core, the pressure created by its enormous gravity forces hydrogen nuclei so close together that they fuse to form helium, releasing huge amounts of energy in the process. The problem for us on Earth is that we can't reproduce the Sun's gravity. To make fusion happen here, we have to compensate by making the fuel far hotter than the centre of the Sun: over a hundred million degrees Celsius, which is several times hotter than the Sun's core.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what fuel do we use? The most promising fuel for a power station is a mixture of two forms of hydrogen, called deuterium and tritium. Deuterium is a heavier form of hydrogen, and it can be extracted from ordinary seawater. There's enough of it in the oceans to supply the world for millions of years. Tritium is more of a problem. It's radioactive, it decays fairly quickly, and there's very little of it in nature. So a fusion power station would have to produce, or breed, its own tritium from lithium inside the reactor itself, and nobody has yet shown that this can be done on the scale required.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: At temperatures of a hundred million degrees, the fuel is no longer an ordinary gas. It becomes a plasma, a state of matter in which the electrons have been separated from the nuclei of the atoms. Obviously, no material container could survive contact with something that hot, so scientists have developed two main ways of holding the fuel in place.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first, and the one that's received most investment, is called magnetic confinement. Because a plasma is made of charged particles, it can be controlled by magnetic fields. The most common design is a doughnut-shaped chamber surrounded by powerful magnets, known as a tokamak. The design was developed in the Soviet Union in the 1950s and 1960s, and the word tokamak is in fact a Russian acronym. For forty years, the most successful machine of this type was JET, the Joint European Torus, near Oxford in England, which operated from 1983 until the end of 2023. In its final experiments, it set a world record for the amount of energy released in a single fusion experiment. Its successor, ITER, is now being built in southern France by a collaboration of around thirty-five countries. ITER is designed to produce ten times more fusion power than the power used to heat the plasma, but it has faced long delays and its cost has risen many times over.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The second approach is called inertial confinement, and it uses lasers instead of magnets. At the National Ignition Facility in California, a hundred and ninety-two lasers are fired at a tiny capsule of fuel, about the size of a peppercorn. The capsule is crushed and heated so quickly that the fuel fuses before it has time to fly apart. In December 2022, scientists there announced that, for the first time, a fusion experiment had released more energy than the laser energy delivered to the fuel. This is known as ignition, and it was a genuine milestone. However, I should point out that the lasers themselves used around a hundred times more electricity from the grid than the experiment produced, so we're still a long way from a power station.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Why go to all this trouble? Well, fusion has some very attractive features. It produces no carbon dioxide. It can't run out of control, because there's no chain reaction as there is in fission. In fact, if anything goes wrong, the plasma simply cools and the reaction stops within seconds. And it doesn't produce the long-lived high-level waste that comes from fission reactors. The walls of the reactor do become radioactive over time, but this material should be safe to handle after decades rather than thousands of years.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The challenges, though, are enormous. Engineers need materials that can survive years of bombardment by the high-energy particles released by fusion. They need to breed tritium reliably. And they need to do all this at a cost that can compete with other sources of electricity. There's an old joke among physicists that fusion is thirty years away, and always will be. In recent years, dozens of private companies have entered the field, attracting billions of dollars of investment and promising much faster progress. Even so, most experts believe fusion is unlikely to make a significant contribution to electricity supplies before the second half of this century, which means it can't replace the need to cut emissions with the technologies we already have.

readingPassages.title: The battery that changed the world
paragraphs: Few inventions have changed daily life as quietly as the rechargeable lithium-ion battery. It powers almost every mobile phone and laptop in the world, as well as the great majority of electric cars, and it is increasingly used to store electricity from wind and solar farms. Yet the technology is surprisingly young. The first lithium-ion batteries went on sale only in 1991, and the three scientists who made them possible were not recognised with a Nobel Prize until 2019.

The basic idea of the battery is much older. In 1800, the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta built a stack of alternating copper and zinc discs separated by pieces of cloth soaked in salt water, and showed that it produced a steady electric current. Volta's 'pile' could not be recharged: once the chemical reactions inside it were complete, it was useless. The first practical rechargeable battery, the lead-acid battery, was invented by the French physicist Gaston Planté in 1859, and versions of it are still used to start the engines of petrol and diesel cars today. Lead-acid batteries are cheap and reliable, but they are also very heavy for the amount of energy they store.

Chemists had long known that lithium, the lightest of all metals, was an attractive material for batteries. Because it gives up its electrons very readily, it can produce a high voltage, and because it is so light, a lithium battery could in principle store far more energy per kilogram than a lead-acid one. The difficulty was that lithium is also extremely reactive. It reacts violently with water and can catch fire when exposed to air. For decades, this made it seem far too dangerous to use in a product that ordinary people would carry around with them.

The breakthrough came in the 1970s, when the oil crisis of 1973 had led governments and companies to search urgently for alternatives to fossil fuels. Stanley Whittingham, a British-born chemist working for the oil company Exxon in the United States, developed a battery in which lithium ions moved into and out of a material called titanium disulphide. His battery produced just over two volts, which was promising. However, its other electrode was made of pure lithium metal, and when the battery was recharged repeatedly, thin threads of lithium grew inside it. These could reach the opposite electrode, causing short circuits and even explosions.

The next steps were taken by two other scientists. In 1980, at the University of Oxford, the American physicist John Goodenough showed that a cathode made of cobalt oxide could produce around four volts, making a much more powerful battery possible. Then, in 1985, the Japanese chemist Akira Yoshino, working for the company Asahi Kasei, replaced the dangerous lithium metal with a form of carbon called petroleum coke, in which lithium ions could be stored. Yoshino's design was lighter and safer, could be recharged hundreds of times, and formed the basis of the first commercial lithium-ion battery, which the Japanese electronics company Sony began selling in 1991.

At first, lithium-ion batteries were used mainly in portable electronic devices such as video cameras, mobile phones and laptop computers, where their light weight was a decisive advantage. Their use in cars came later, and it was made possible by a dramatic fall in price. According to industry analysts, the average cost of a lithium-ion battery pack fell by roughly ninety per cent between 2010 and 2020, largely as a result of mass production and steady improvements in manufacturing. As a result, electric cars, which had once been expensive curiosities, began to compete seriously with petrol and diesel vehicles.

The same fall in prices has made it possible to use batteries on a very large scale to support electricity grids. One of the best-known early examples is the Hornsdale Power Reserve in South Australia, which was built by the American company Tesla and began operating in 2017. At the time, it was the largest lithium-ion battery installation in the world. Such facilities can respond to sudden changes in supply or demand within a fraction of a second, which helps to keep the grid stable as a growing share of electricity comes from wind and solar power, whose output varies with the weather.

Lithium-ion batteries are not without problems. Mining lithium, cobalt and nickel can damage the environment and, in some places, has been linked to poor working conditions. Damaged batteries can overheat and catch fire. Researchers are therefore exploring alternatives, including sodium-ion batteries, which use a far more abundant element, and solid-state batteries, which replace the flammable liquid inside current batteries with a solid material. When the Nobel Prize was finally awarded, Goodenough was 97, making him the oldest person ever to receive one. He lived until 2023, by which time the invention he had helped to create had become one of the foundations of the world's effort to move away from fossil fuels.

readingPassages.title: Hydrogen: fuel of the future?
paragraphs: Hydrogen is the simplest and most abundant element in the universe, and for well over a century it has been described as the fuel of the future. In The Mysterious Island, published in the 1870s, the French novelist Jules Verne had one of his characters predict that water would one day be used as fuel, with the hydrogen and oxygen it contains providing an inexhaustible source of heat and light. When hydrogen is burned or used in a fuel cell, the only by-product is water. It is hardly surprising, then, that it has attracted renewed interest as countries try to cut their carbon emissions. Whether it will play a central role in the energy system, or a much more limited one, remains a subject of intense debate.

Hydrogen was first recognised as a distinct substance in 1766 by the English scientist Henry Cavendish, who called it 'inflammable air'. In 1783, the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier gave it its modern name, from the Greek for 'water-former', after showing that it produced water when burned. Because it is the lightest of all gases, hydrogen was soon used to fill balloons, and in the early twentieth century it lifted the great passenger airships. That era ended abruptly in 1937, when the German airship Hindenburg caught fire while landing in New Jersey, killing thirty-six people. The disaster gave hydrogen a reputation for danger that it has never entirely lost.

What many people do not realise is that hydrogen is already a major industrial product. Nearly one hundred million tonnes are produced each year, mostly for refining oil and for making ammonia, the basis of most of the world's nitrogen fertilisers. Almost all of it, however, is made from fossil fuels, mainly by reacting natural gas with steam at high temperatures, a process that releases large quantities of carbon dioxide. As a result, hydrogen production today is responsible for more greenhouse gas emissions than some entire countries. Before hydrogen can help to solve the climate problem, in other words, the existing industry must itself be cleaned up.

To describe the different ways of making hydrogen, the industry has adopted a system of colours. Hydrogen made from natural gas without any attempt to capture the carbon dioxide is known as grey hydrogen. If the carbon dioxide is captured and stored underground, the result is called blue hydrogen, although critics point out that capture rates are often lower than promised and that methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, can leak from gas wells and pipelines. Green hydrogen is produced by electrolysis, in which an electric current from renewable sources such as wind or solar power is used to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. Green hydrogen produces almost no emissions, but it currently costs considerably more than grey hydrogen and makes up only a tiny fraction of total production.

Even when it has been produced cleanly, hydrogen is awkward to handle. Although it contains more energy per kilogram than petrol, it contains very little energy per litre at normal pressure, because it is so light. To be useful as a fuel for vehicles, it must either be compressed to around seven hundred times atmospheric pressure or cooled to minus 253 degrees Celsius to turn it into a liquid. Both processes consume a significant amount of energy. Hydrogen's tiny molecules can also escape through very small gaps, and over time the gas can make some metals brittle, so pipelines and storage tanks must be specially designed.

A further drawback is efficiency. Every time energy is converted from one form to another, some of it is lost. When renewable electricity is used to make hydrogen, which is then compressed, transported and turned back into electricity in a fuel cell, much of the original energy disappears along the way. For this reason, a battery electric car can travel roughly two to three times as far as a hydrogen fuel-cell car on the same amount of renewable electricity. This helps to explain why, despite years of government support in countries such as Japan and South Korea, sales of hydrogen cars remain tiny compared with those of battery electric cars.

None of this means that hydrogen has no future. There are some activities for which batteries are unlikely to be practical and for which few other low-carbon options exist. Steelmaking is one. Conventional blast furnaces use coal both as a fuel and to remove oxygen from iron ore, but hydrogen can do the same chemical job, producing water instead of carbon dioxide. In 2021, a Swedish project known as HYBRIT delivered what it described as the world's first steel made using fossil-free hydrogen to the vehicle manufacturer Volvo. Hydrogen, or fuels made from it such as ammonia, may also be needed for long-distance shipping and for storing energy over many months, which batteries cannot yet do economically.

In 2021, the energy analyst Michael Liebreich proposed what he called a 'hydrogen ladder', a ranking of possible uses from those where clean hydrogen is essential to those where other technologies are likely to win. Fertiliser production and steelmaking are near the top; heating homes and powering cars are near the bottom. The ladder has been widely discussed because it captures a broader point. Hydrogen is a valuable but limited resource, and the challenge for governments is not to promote it everywhere, but to direct it towards the places where it will make the greatest difference.

readingPassages.title: Should nuclear power be part of the answer?
paragraphs: Few energy sources divide opinion as sharply as nuclear power. To its supporters, it is a reliable, low-carbon source of electricity that can run day and night regardless of the weather, and that the world cannot afford to ignore if it is serious about climate change. To its opponents, it is expensive, slow to build and potentially catastrophic when things go wrong, and it leaves behind waste that will remain dangerous for thousands of years. Nuclear power currently generates just under a tenth of the world's electricity, so the question of whether that share should grow or shrink is far from academic.

The strongest evidence of what nuclear power can achieve comes from France. After the oil crisis of 1973 exposed the country's dependence on imported oil, the French government launched an ambitious programme, often called the Messmer plan after the prime minister of the time, to build dozens of reactors in little more than fifteen years. Today nuclear power provides around two thirds of France's electricity, and its power sector produces far less carbon dioxide per unit of electricity than those of neighbouring countries that rely more heavily on fossil fuels. The French experience suggests that when reactors are built in large numbers to a standard design, costs and construction times can be kept under control.

Public fear of nuclear power owes much to two accidents. In 1986, an explosion at the Chernobyl plant in Ukraine, then part of the Soviet Union, spread radioactive material across much of Europe, and a large area around the plant remains largely closed today. In 2011, an earthquake and tsunami in Japan disabled the cooling systems at the Fukushima Daiichi plant, causing meltdowns in three reactors. Yet the number of deaths directly caused by radiation at Fukushima was very small, and studies have found that the hurried evacuation of the surrounding area, particularly of elderly and sick people, caused far more deaths than radiation itself. When deaths from accidents and air pollution are measured per unit of electricity generated, nuclear power turns out to be among the safest sources of energy, comparable with wind and solar power and far safer than coal.

Fukushima nevertheless had dramatic political consequences, and not only in Japan, which shut down all of its reactors for safety checks and restarted only some of them years later. In Germany, the government responded by bringing forward its plans to phase out nuclear power, and the country's last three reactors were closed in April 2023. Germany has expanded its use of renewable energy enormously, but critics argue that, by closing working nuclear plants before its coal plants, it burned more coal than it otherwise would have done, increasing both carbon emissions and air pollution.

The most serious practical objection to nuclear power today concerns cost and time. Several recent projects in Europe and North America have run years behind schedule and far over budget. The Olkiluoto 3 reactor in Finland is a striking example: construction began in 2005, with completion planned for 2009, but the reactor did not begin regular electricity production until 2023. Meanwhile, the cost of solar panels, wind turbines and batteries has fallen dramatically, so that in many countries new renewable capacity is now considerably cheaper to build. Supporters of nuclear power respond that such comparisons ignore the cost of backing up wind and solar power when the weather is calm or cloudy.

Then there is the question of waste. The volume of highly radioactive waste is relatively small, but it must be kept isolated from people and the environment for many thousands of years. For decades, no country had a permanent solution, and spent fuel was kept in temporary stores, often at the power stations themselves. Finland, again, has taken the lead. At Onkalo, near Olkiluoto, it has built a repository in which spent fuel will be sealed in copper canisters and buried in solid rock more than four hundred metres underground. It is expected to be the first facility of its kind in the world to begin operating.

Many hopes for the future rest on new technologies. Small modular reactors, which would be built in factories and transported to their sites, are intended to reduce the costs and delays that have troubled large projects, although only a handful have yet been built anywhere in the world, and none in large numbers. Fusion power, which would join atoms together rather than splitting them, promises abundant energy with far less long-lived waste, but even its supporters admit that it is unlikely to supply significant amounts of electricity for several decades.

In my view, the case against nuclear power on grounds of safety is much weaker than its reputation suggests, and the closure of reactors that were operating safely, while coal plants continued to run, was a mistake. The objection based on cost, however, is a serious one, and supporters of nuclear power too often dismiss it. Money spent on a reactor that takes fifteen years to build cannot also be spent on wind and solar farms that could be producing clean electricity within two or three. The sensible conclusion, I believe, is that existing reactors should be kept running for as long as they are safe, and that new ones should be built only where they can be delivered on time and at a reasonable cost. Nor should the waste problem be seen as unsolvable: Finland has shown that it is a question of political will rather than technical possibility.
